phonemes.desc: Short epsilon with rough breathing followed by rho — the name begins with a rush, like a messenger arriving.
Mu plus long eta and sigma — the long vowel gives the name its final clarity.

pronunciation.approximation: 'her-MACE' — the first syllable is quick and breathy; the second is long, level, and carries the accent.

pronunciation.note: Hermês is Tier 1 because the Greek Ἑρμῆς contains both stress (circumflex on the long η) and length (η). The circumflex form Hermês is the ideal; Hermēs is the macron-only LSJ convention. The name's boundary-marker etymology suits the god of thresholds.

domains.title: The Messenger
domains.subtitle: Travel, Commerce, Thievery, and Boundaries
domains.lead: Hermês is the fastest, cleverest, and most adaptable of the gods. He moves between Olympus, earth, and the underworld; he protects travelers, merchants, thieves, and heralds alike. Where there is a boundary — a door, a road, a market, a grave — there is Hermês.

cards.name: Messenger of the Gods
cards.desc: He carries Zeús's commands and guides souls to the underworld.

cards.name: Boundaries and Thresholds
cards.desc: Herms marked property lines, roads, and doorways; he protects those who cross from one place to another.

cards.name: Commerce and Exchange
cards.desc: Patron of merchants, markets, and honest — or clever — dealing.

cards.name: Trickster and Thief
cards.desc: On his first day he stole Apóllōn's cattle; his cunning is as divine as his duty.

mythology.lead: Hermês's myths celebrate intelligence in motion. Born at dawn, by nightfall he has invented music, stolen a herd, and talked his way out of both — and Zeús rewards him with every boundary-crossing office: herald, trader, guide of the dead. Every threshold in the Greek world — door, road, market, grave — stood under his sign.

myths.title: Born in a Cave on Mount Cyllene
myths.text: The Homeric Hymn to Hermes (1–104) stages the most precocious first day in mythology. Maia's child is born at dawn in a cave on Mount Cyllene; by midday he has found a tortoise, stretched gut-strings across its shell, and invented the lyre; by evening he slips out to Pieria and steals fifty of Apóllōn's cattle, driving them backward and binding brushwood to his own feet so the tracks deceive. Back home he sacrifices two cows, divides the meat into twelve portions for the gods, and — a newborn — slips into his cradle, where Apóllōn finds him wrapped in swaddling with a sly look in his eye. Accused before Zeús, the infant's defense is flawless comedy: he was born only yesterday, he says, his feet are tender, and the ground is rough. The hymn makes theft the first technology of intelligence and the lyre its first recompense.

myths.title: The Lyre for the Herd
myths.text: Zeús orders the cattle returned, and the confrontation on Mount Cyllene becomes the charter of exchange. Hermês offers the lyre; Apóllōn, hearing it, is enchanted, and trades the whole herd for the instrument, adding his golden staff and the gift of prophecy from the bee-maidens of Parnassus (Homeric Hymn 434–568). The brothers cut a covenant, and Zeús then crowns the treaty: Hermês is confirmed in his honors — god of flocks, of markets, of roads, and of secret knowledge. The myth is the Greeks' own origin story for the market: theft, confronted, is transformed into trade; what was taken is returned as an instrument of pleasure, and the thief becomes the patron of honest dealing. Hermês is the only god whose portfolio begins with a crime and ends with a handshake.

myths.title: Guide of Souls and Bearer of Moly
myths.text: Hermês alone walks all three realms without penalty. In Odyssey 24 he leads the suitors' souls down to the underworld, golden wand in hand — the psychopompos in his oldest surviving role. In Odyssey 10 Zeús sends him to Circe's island with the herb moly, black-rooted and white-flowered, 'hard for mortal men to dig, but gods can do all things,' and the god's intervention saves Odysseus from the witch's potion. The titles cluster: Argeiphontes, slayer of Argos; Diaktoros, the guide; Eriounios, the helpful. Hermês is the god of the threshold in every sense — the doorway between houses, between cities, between languages, and between the living and the dead. Where a being must pass from one order into another, the Greeks sent ahead the god who had himself talked his way from cradle to Olympus in a single day.

myths.title: Words Against a Hundred Eyes
myths.text: Homer's favorite title for Hermês is Argeiphontes, 'slayer of Argos' (Iliad 24.24, 153). The deed it commemorates is Ovid's masterpiece of narrative seduction (Metamorphoses 1.668–723): sent by Zeús to free Io, guarded by the hundred-eyed Argos, Hermês disguises himself as a shepherd and tells the long, wandering story of Syrinx, the nymph who fled Pan's pursuit and was changed into reeds — until, one by one, the hundred eyes of Argos fall shut, and Hermês strikes, sheathing his sword before Argos can even reach for his own. Ovid makes language itself the weapon: the god of speech conquers the god of vigilance by telling him a better story than waking. The myth belongs to Hermês's deepest stratum — intelligence defeating watchfulness, words defeating eyes — and it is the reason every herald's staff and every fine-spoken embassy in the Greek world moved under his sign.

myths.title: Battos and the Telling Stone
myths.text: Hermês's one punitive myth is a parable about the word. Stealing Apóllōn's cattle, the young god is seen by an old man, Battos, and bribes him to silence with the promise of a cow. Hermês returns in disguise, offers Battos a cow and a bull if he will reveal the thief — and the old man takes the second bribe, whereupon Hermês turns him into the index, the 'telling stone': a landmark that reports everything it sees (Ovid, Metamorphoses 2.676–707; Antoninus Liberalis 23, preserving Nicander and Corinna). The story is Hermês's counterweight to the lyre myth: the god who invented trade punishes the man who sells the same secret twice. In a theology where Hermês governs every exchange — of goods, of messages, of souls — the unfaithful tongue is the one treasure that cannot be traded without loss. Even his vengeance is a lesson in exchange rates.

lore.syncretism: The Romans identified Hermês with Mercurius, the god of commerce and travel, whose name gives us 'merchant' and 'mercury.' The planet Mercury, swift in its orbit, bears his name. In Egypt he was fused with Thoth, the ibis-headed god of writing and wisdom, producing the figure of Hermes Trismegistus, central to Hellenistic and Renaissance occultism. The caduceus, though often confused with the rod of Asclepius, remains a global symbol of diplomacy and medicine.
lore.culturalLegacy: Hermês is the god of everything that moves: messages, money, travelers, thieves, and souls. The herm was one of the most common religious objects in Athens; every doorway and road was under his protection. In philosophy, Hermes Trismegistus became a founder of alchemy and Hermeticism. Modern concepts of communication, commerce, and even the internet — a network of boundaries crossed at speed — would have seemed to the Greeks like the domain of Hermês. Restoring Hermês restores the name of the god who first made exchange possible.
lore.extendedMeditation:
Hermês is the god of the in-between moment: the handshake, the border crossing, the message sent but not yet received. He is neither Olympian splendor nor chthonic dread but the quick intelligence that moves between them. The Greeks trusted him on roads because they knew that roads are dangerous, and danger requires a clever companion.

Every time we send a message, make a trade, or cross a threshold, we repeat the gestures Hermês invented. The internet is his latest domain: a vast network of exchanges across boundaries, some honest, some thieving, all swift. The restoration of his name in Unicode is fitting: he would have approved of a script that lets any language travel instantly.
lore.archaeology: Thousands of herms—four-sided pillars topped with Hermes' head and genitals—stood at doorways, crossroads, and gymnasia across Athens; the mutilation of the herms in 415 BCE is recorded by Thucydides and left numerous surviving examples. The Hermes of Praxiteles (Archaeological Museum of Olympia) is a fourth-century BCE marble of the god carrying the infant Dionysos. The herm of Andros and the Archanes herms illustrate his role as boundary guardian.
